item.title: Suno CEO: AI Could Reinvent How We Experience Music
item.description:
Suno CEO and Co-Founder Mikey Shulman says AI could transform music from a largely passive experience into one where listeners actively create, remix and collaborate with their favorite artists. With more than 100 million users and partnerships across the music industry, Shulman discusses Suno’s in-house AI models, opportunities around licensing artists’ voices and music, and why he believes AI can expand the music business. He joins Ed Ludlow on "Bloomberg Tech." (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Apple Wants to Take Over Your Home. Is Siri AI Ready?
item.description:
In the premiere episode of Power On, Mark Gurman and Bloomberg Tech Editor Vlad Savov discuss two of Apple’s most anticipated Fall releases. First, Mark shares his massive scoop on Apple’s long awaited push into the home and what makes their Siri AI-powered devices different from other smart home options. Then, Mark and Vlad consider if upgrading to the new iPhone 18 is worth it and question Apple’s reliance on influencer marketing. Have a question for Mark? Email us at poweron@bloomberg.net or join the Power On Discord Subscribe to the Power On Newsletter at https://www.bloomberg.com/poweron (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Carlyle Warns on AI Hype and Credit Risk Ahead
item.description:
Amid the AI boom, private credit is pouring into data centers and hyperscalers, but the risks are real. Carlyle's Co-President Mark Jenkins joins Bloomberg Open Interest with a warning that concentration in a single hot theme can mirror the "SaaS apocalypse," where everything looked diversified until volatility hit. He breaks down where AI credit risk is building, how complex data‑center contracts can fail, and why old‑school diversification still matters more than AI hype. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Are We Losing Control of AI? What’s Driving New Fears
item.description:
For years, as artificial intelligence has evolved from the stuff of sci-fi movies to an app ordinary people have installed on their phones, tech leaders and some AI insiders have talked about the potential for it to escape human control and wreak havoc on society. Those fears have become impossible to ignore in recent weeks, driven by advances in the technology, a series of cybersecurity breaches involving AI agents, and new warnings from rank-and-file AI staffers.

The software firm — which is a subsidiary of Mozilla.org, a nonprofit that promotes openness, innovation and participation on the internet — recently appointed a new chief executive to help revamp its strategy. Eric Muhlheim, who became CFO in 2021 after stints at Buzzfeed and Disney, talks about balancing mission and returns, diversifying Mozilla’s revenue streams and AI costs. Mozilla CFO Eric Muhlheim and Bloomberg's Nina Trentmann discuss the impact of AI on capex spend, corporate strategy, and company principles in our CFO Briefing. They speak with Bloomberg Businessweek Daily hosts Carol Massar and Tim Stenovec. Correct: Updates description, headline (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: AI Is Upending the Lives of People Who Do Social Media Professionally
item.description:
Social media is really strange these days: Increasingly, our feeds are starting to look uncanny, as AI slop proliferates all over the Internet. And for the professionals who are tasked with making content, whether it is social media managers or creators, it has been a head-spinning time of change. In this conversation, recorded at the Vermont in Hollywood, we get a primer on social media's AI era with two veteran Internet commentators, Rachel Karten (social media consultant and the author of the Link in Bio newsletter) and Taylor Lorenz (founder of User Mag). We discuss why people are afraid to admit that they love some genres of slop, why the AI discourse is evolving so rapidly, and whether our time online is moving away from scrolling feeds to engaging with chatbots. (Source: Bloomberg)

Iran meanwhile laid down “firm positions” for the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, including the US immediately lifting a naval blockade, unfreezing Iranian assets and ending the war “on all fronts”. Speaking to Bloomberg TV, Lizzy Galbraith, senior political economist at Aberdeen said that the fact that talks are happening is better than no talks, but stressed that the key issue is whether either side has actually changed its negotiating position. She noted that the U.S., including Trump and Steve Witkoff, has sounded upbeat, while Iran has framed the meeting as a chance to restate its own demands. This plan could reshape traditional market structure after crypto legislation failed a key Senate vote on Tuesday. Also affecting the crypto space, Bitcoin surged past $85,000 to its highest since late-January, extending a sharp rebound as falling oil prices and a broader return of risk appetite helped cryptocurrencies move past setbacks on US crypto legislation and monetary policy. The original cryptocurrency climbed as much as 6.5% to $86,331 in New York trading, almost $10,000 above the lows touched last week after the Clarity Act stalled and the Federal Reserve raised interest rates. Even after that rebound, Bitcoin remains roughly a third below its record last October. Nathan Dean speaks with Bloomberg's Joe Mathieu on Balance of Power. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.description:
Rob Barnett, Bloomberg Intelligence Senior Energy and Commodities Analyst, joined Bloomberg's Paul Sweeney and Scarlet Fu to discuss the latest in oil. Oil fell below $100, heading for its longest run of declines since June, as robust flows through the Strait of Hormuz and diplomacy around the US-Iran war tamed a recent rally. Brent, the global benchmark, fell as much as 4.2% while West Texas Intermediate futures were down over 5% to trade near $95 a barrel. Satellite data showed that Saudi Arabia’s observed oil loadings from inside the Persian Gulf jumped over the weekend, with the highest number of ships seen at the nation’s main Persian Gulf port since June. It’s a sign the kingdom has pivoted back toward Hormuz after the shutdown of a key cross-country pipeline to the Red Sea earlier this month following drone attacks. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: How LA Is Becoming America's New Industrial Tech Hub
item.description:
The story you hear nowadays is that America is struggling to make things and can't compete with China when it comes to advanced manufacturing. But of course, there's tons of high-tech stuff being produced in the US, and more and more companies are doing it out of Southern California, with factories sprouting up around Los Angeles to build things like precision metal parts and jet engines. Two founders who are actively engaged in building things in LA are Tom Mueller, founder of Impulse Space (and Employee No. 1 at SpaceX), as well as Hadrian founder Chris Power. Impulse Space is building in-space transport vehicles while Hadrian is creating autonomous factories. This episode was recorded live at the Vermont Hollywood, as part of our first ever Odd Lots live show in LA. We talk to Chris and Tom about how the US lost its manufacturing edge and why LA is becoming a destination for people who want to make and build hardware. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.description:
Merryn Somerset Webb speaks with Daniel Susskind, senior research associate at the Institute for Ethics in AI at the University of Oxford and a member of the UK government’s expert panel on artificial intelligence and the future of work. AI is expected to transform the job market, potentially upending many of the traditional educational pathways that have long led students into established professions. As those routes begin to look increasingly uncertain, how should young people prepare for the world of work that awaits them? In his book, What Should My Children Do?, Susskind seeks to answer that question, offering a framework for how children — and adults — can best prepare for an evolving labor market with AI at its center. item.title: India’s Silicon Valley Is Straining Under Its Own Growth
item.description:
Bangalore helped turn India into a global hub for software services, tech talent and outsourcing, building an ecosystem that now supports multinational firms, domestic startups and capital. But the city’s success has also become one of its biggest weaknesses. India still lacks the depth of capital available in the US and China, while Bangalore’s physical infrastructure has struggled to keep pace with private-sector growth. At the same time, southern India’s rising economic power is colliding with demographic and political shifts that could threaten its representation in the country’s Central Government, which helps support the growth that cities like Bangalore have enjoyed. This version corrects a map of India. (Source: Bloomberg)

Gene Sykes has seen multiple deal cycles come and go over his multi-decade career at the firm. The co-head of mergers and acquisitions has worked on famous transactions like Comcast's purchase of Universal and Disney's buyout of Pixar. In addition to being "the most-influential M&A banker you've never heard of," as New York magazine has put it, he has also spearheaded Los Angeles's successful bid to bring the Olympic Games to the city in 2028. item.author: Neil Jerome Morales

item.title: There's a Mind-Boggling Number of Rich People in America
item.description:
In 2014, the economists Owen Zidar and Eric Zwick were asked by the Treasury to conduct a study on the tax burden of private business owners. It was tricky to figure out how much these sorts of business owners — auto dealers, contractors, the like — actually owed in taxes: After Reagan's 1986 tax reforms, pass-through businesses and other accounting tricks became widespread enough to obscure this class of wealthy Americans hiding in plain sight. The research they conducted led to their new book The Everywhere Millionaire: Who Is Really Rich in America and How They Got There, and one of their central findings is that there are about three million private business owners who have an average wealth of around $25 million. They call this group “Main Street Millionaires” and their influence on the economy and politics in the US is considerable. We speak with Zidar and Zwick about how they measured the actual number of rich people in America. (Source: Bloomberg)

Leaders of Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceX and Google DeepMind put forward the need for self-regulation checks on growth that give AI models more control. Meanwhile, Microsoft, Amazon and Meta said they're developing tools to check, control and regulate AI risks as US President Donald Trump called the alerts a "hoax". The call for caution saw a rotation out of tech stocks at the start of the week as investors questioned whether there's a need to reprice the pace of the booming AI buildout. (Source: Bloomberg)

Bharat Ramamurti, Former Deputy Director of the National Economic Council, says President Donald Trump’s proposed $5,000 dividend checks would be “unequivocally inflationary” and could force the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates further. Ramamurti says that continued rate hikes could push unemployment higher and that, if oil prices keep rising at the same time, the US risks ending up with stagflation alongside a weakening labor market. He speaks with Kailey Leinz and Joe Mathieu on Bloomberg’s "Balance of Power." (Source: Bloomberg)

item.author: Bloomberg

item.title: Bloomberg Businessweek Daily: OpenAI Safety Incidents (Podcast)
item.description:
OpenAI shared several undisclosed incidents of its AI models misbehaving and unveiled a new framework for tracking and disclosing such occurrences going forward. Some of the previously unreported instances included OpenAI’s technologies concealing and fabricating information in order to return results, the company said in a blog post Wednesday. The ChatGPT maker has faced increased scrutiny since saying in July that some of its most advanced AI models had breached the systems of an external software company, Hugging Face. None of the newly disclosed misalignment incidents involved a hack or breach of a third party, OpenAI said in a separate statement. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Sen. Armstrong Says Energy Crunch Shows Infrastructure Gaps
item.description:
Sen. Alan Armstrong (R-OK) says the current energy crunch is exposing the cost of constrained infrastructure and strengthening the case for permitting reform. Sen. Armstrong points to the sharp gap in diesel prices between Oklahoma and California and the attack on Saudi pipeline infrastructure as examples of how limited capacity can leave consumers more vulnerable to price shocks. Sen. Armstrong says he is encouraged Congress could still act on permitting reform before the end of the session. He speaks with Kailey Leinz and Joe Mathieu on Bloomberg’s "Balance of Power." (Source: Bloomberg)

AI pioneer Andrew Ng is pushing back against renewed warnings that increasingly powerful models could pose an existential threat to humanity, calling those fears “much more science fiction than science.” He argues that AI systems will never be perfectly predictable, but that testing, safeguards, and engineering, can make them safer over time. He also warns that broadly slowing AI development could also slow progress on safety. He joins Ed Ludlow on "Bloomberg Tech." (Source: Bloomberg)

item.author: Bloomberg

item.title: AI ‘Existential Risk’ Is Close to Zero: Databricks CEO
item.description:
Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi is pushing back on fears that AI poses an existential threat to humanity, calling that risk “close to zero” while warning that the technology presents a very real and growing cybersecurity challenge. He discusses why AI is dramatically shortening the time it takes attackers to exploit vulnerabilities, how Databricks is preparing for those threats, and why the current period of rapid technological change reinforces his preference to keep the company private for now. He joins Ed Ludlow on "Bloomberg Tech." (Source: Bloomberg)

On this episode of Stock Movers: - Generac (GNRC) shares are jumping after the company and Amazon execute a long-term supply agreement, with initial deliveries of backup generators expected to total $2.4b in 2027, 2028. - CoreWeave (CRWV) is the most actively traded stock in the premarket as it kicked off a fresh round of fundraising that includes a $3 billion convertible bond issue and a vehicle for potential share sales. - Lockheed Martin (LMT) shares are moving on news the Pentagon and Lockheed Martin have struck a framework agreement for a multi-year production contract for the Joint Advanced Tactical Missile, or JATM. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Clara Wu Tsai on the NY Liberty, Rise of the WNBA | The David Rubenstein Show
item.description:
Clara Wu Tsai is one of the most influential sports owners and philanthropists today. In 2019, she and her husband, Joe Tsai, bought the New York Liberty, where she helped transform the franchise into a WNBA championship team by investing in players, facilities, management and the fan experience. Wu Tsai, who also co-owns the Brooklyn Nets, explains why sports have become a legitimate asset class and why live sports are increasingly valuable in the age of AI. She also reflects on her journey from growing up in Kansas as the daughter of immigrants from Taiwan, to building a career in business as well as her philanthropy, and the lessons she's learned about leadership, opportunity and success. Wu Tsai joins David Rubenstein for the premiere episode of The David Rubenstein Show: Peer to Peer Conversations, Season 12. This interview was recorded June 4, in Brooklyn, New York. (Source: Bloomberg)
